selene.14: At the Moon's south pole the Sun barely grazes the horizon and the Earth keeps disappearing behind the terrain. A mission needs both: light for its solar panels and the Earth in sight to communicate. SELENE compares landing sites and dates and shows where the Sun and the Earth sit over each site's real horizon, with a site ranking, an illumination heat map, a 3D Moon and a printable report.

p.selene.desc: SELENE, a landing-site explorer for the Moon's south pole. NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
d.selene.1.1: At the lunar south pole the Sun barely clears the horizon and the Earth rises and sets over the month. A few kilometres or a few days can completely change how much energy a mission gets and when it can talk to Earth.
d.selene.1.2: The NASA tools that hold this data (JPL Horizons, Quickmap, Moon Trek) are built for detailed analysis and are hard to use for quick comparisons. The challenge asked for something intuitive for mission planners, teachers and the general public.
d.selene.2.1: Site and date ranking, with Overall, Science, Communication and Light categories.
d.selene.2.2: Curated sites (Shackleton, Malapert, Cabeus, IM-1 Odysseus, Chandrayaan-3, Chang’e 4 and Apollo 11), each with the source of its coordinates, or any point on the map.
d.selene.2.3: 3D and 2D Moon with layers for sunlight, Earth visibility, viability, night and elevation.
d.selene.2.4: 360° panorama with the measured terrain and the paths of the Sun and the Earth, playable or draggable.
d.selene.2.5: Energy and communication metrics: hours of light, link coverage, longest night, outages and sunrises computed to a 5-second tolerance.
d.selene.2.6: Viability with editable assumptions (batteries, minimum communication, relay satellite), based on NASA requirements for Artemis.
d.selene.2.7: Side-by-side comparison of two sites and a printable report.
d.selene.3.1: Azimuth, elevation and apparent radius of the Sun and Earth from each site, hour by hour, from November 2026 to December 2027 (DE441).
d.selene.3.2: LDEM_60S_240M, LDEM_128 and LDEM_16 elevation models for each site’s real horizon and the heat map.
d.selene.3.3: LROC WAC mosaic and LOLA elevation for the 2D and 3D views.
d.selene.3.4: Landing-site coordinates, each with its source inside the app.
d.selene.4.1: Vite and modular JavaScript, no framework, with three.js for the Moon. The astronomy lives in one folder and the interface, which only displays, in another. Ephemerides and horizons are processed ahead of time and published as static files, so the site needs no server.
d.selene.4.2: It’s bilingual and has a colour-blind palette, high contrast, a reduced-motion mode, keyboard controls and a guided tour. Every selection is kept in the URL so it can be shared.
d.selene.4.3: Every task was done in its own branch, and every decision was logged together with the alternatives we dropped.
d.selene.6.1: It’s a concept design for comparing scenarios, not a precision engineering tool.
d.selene.6.2: Outside the ephemeris range (November 2026 to December 2027) it uses an approximate model and says so on screen.
d.selene.6.3: For custom points the horizon is computed at lower resolution and flagged as approximate.
d.selene.6.4: It’s designed for desktop, from 1200 px wide.
p.parkex.desc: ParkEx: real-time parking monitoring with automatic checks of accessible bays.
d.parkex.1.1: In a private car park (a building, a mall, a clinic) people drive through whole levels looking for a space. Meanwhile accessible bays are often taken by cars without a permit, and the operator has no practical way to find out.
d.parkex.1.2: ParkEx tackles both with low-cost hardware: one ultrasonic sensor per bay, a camera only on the reserved ones, and a website with the live map and an alerts panel.
d.parkex.2.1: No external registries. The permit is recognised by the DI mark printed on the Uruguayan plate itself.
d.parkex.2.2: Several photos per event and consensus between readings to rule out OCR errors.
d.parkex.2.3: The system doesn’t penalise. A doubtful reading is marked “not verifiable” and never raises an alert; alerts go to human review.
d.parkex.2.4: Privacy by design. The plate is never stored as text: it leaves the car-park computer only as an HMAC-SHA256, and images are processed in memory and discarded.
d.parkex.2.5: Sensors without credentials. Each bay’s Arduino has no WiFi and no token; all connectivity lives on a single computer acting as a bridge.
d.parkex.3.1: The Arduino measures distance with the HC-SR04, decides whether the bay is taken and writes it to the serial port.
d.parkex.3.2: The serial bridge (Node.js) turns each line into an API request.
d.parkex.3.3: The API (Express) stores the event in Supabase, and Supabase Realtime notifies the connected browsers.
d.parkex.3.4: If the bay is reserved, the reader (Java, OpenCV and Tesseract) takes several photos, reads the plate, looks for the mark and reports only the hash and the result.
d.parkex.3.5: If the car has no mark, an alert shows up in the panel without reloading the page.
d.parkex.4.1: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, SVG floor plan
d.parkex.5.1: Presented at UTEC’s 3rd Academic Week of Logistics Engineering (Northern Regional Technological Institute, Rivera, 6–8 October 2026), where it won Best presentation and Academic excellence.
d.parkex.5.2: The abstract is published in the event’s book of abstracts: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23377101.
d.parkex.6.1: Joaquín Castro, Catalina Ligüera, Luciano Bazzano, Facundo Duarte and Lucio Facchin
d.parkex.6.3: Working prototype, tested end to end on a real parking bay.

p.escaneo.desc: IP Scan: a Java network scanner that pings in parallel and cross-checks the ARP table.
d.escaneo.1.1: Takes a network in CIDR notation and validates every octet and the prefix (/0 to /32).
d.escaneo.1.2: Works out the addresses in the range; up to /30 it leaves out the network and broadcast addresses.
d.escaneo.1.3: Pings all of them in parallel, with a pool of up to 100 threads and a 1 s timeout per address.
d.escaneo.1.4: Reads the ARP table with arp -a and, if that fails, with ip neigh. It understands Linux, macOS and Windows output.
d.escaneo.1.5: Combines both and shows IP, MAC and status, with the number of active hosts and how long it took.
d.escaneo.2.1: Besides the terminal it has a web mode: the JDK’s own HTTP server serves the page and a POST /api/escanear API that takes the network as JSON. If the range is over 1024 addresses, it asks for confirmation before scanning.
d.escaneo.3.1: If it detects it’s running inside Flatpak (for example, from an IDE installed that way), it runs ping and arp on the host with flatpak-spawn --host; otherwise the results would come back empty.
d.escaneo.4.1: Reads the network, runs the scan and prints the table
d.escaneo.4.2: Validates the notation and generates the addresses
d.escaneo.4.4: Reads and normalises the ARP table
d.escaneo.4.6: Detects Flatpak and wraps the commands
p.cinniminies.desc: Cinniminies: the ordering site for a cinnamon roll business in Paysandú.
d.cinniminies.1.1: A small bakery in Paysandú with no shop: we bake for Saturdays and every box is put together by hand. The site has to sell and, above all, organise the orders that used to arrive scattered across WhatsApp and Instagram.
d.cinniminies.2.1: Box builder: 6 or 12 rolls, or a custom box of 3 to 12, filled with the flavours you pick.
d.cinniminies.2.2: Cart that tells you when the box is full.
d.cinniminies.2.3: Form with live validation: for example, the WhatsApp number has to be a 9-digit Uruguayan mobile starting with 09.
d.cinniminies.2.4: Pick-up or delivery, with shipping added to the total.
d.cinniminies.2.5: Payment in cash or by bank transfer: every order gets a number to use as the reference, and the receipt can be uploaded.
d.cinniminies.2.6: Discount codes for people who refer someone.
d.cinniminies.3.1: The FAQ answers what people actually search for (“where can I buy cinnamon rolls in Paysandú?”, flavours, delivery, payment), so the site also works for local search.
d.cinniminies.4.1: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript; on the server side, Vercel Functions and Supabase, plus push notifications.
